# Introduction

In this lab you'll work with hotel cancellations.
The data describe the demand of two different types of hotels.
Each observation represents a hotel booking between July 1, 2015 and August 31, 2017.
Some bookings were canceled (`is_canceled = 1`) and others were kept, i.e., the guests checked into the hotel (`is_canceled = 0`).
You can view the code book for all variables [here](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/master/data/2020/2020-02-11/readme.md).

## Learning objectives

By the end of the lab, you will...

-   Prepare a dataset for modeling: recode an outcome as a factor, filter out data quality issues, and split the data into training and testing sets.
-   Fit logistic regression models and interpret their coefficients.
-   Compute predicted probabilities by hand and with R, and classify observations.
-   Evaluate a classifier on a testing set.

## Checking your work

This lab is **autograded**.
That changes two things about how you work:

1.  **Answers go into named objects.**
    Each question below tells you exactly what to name your answer (e.g., "save the model as `cancel_fit`"), and the template's code cells already contain placeholders such as `cancel_fit <- NULL` with a short comment describing what goes there.
    Replace the `NULL` (or `NA`) with your code, but **do not change the object names**.
    The autograder looks for these exact names; an answer stored under a different name receives no credit, even if the code is correct.

2.  **You can check your answers as you go.**
    After each question, the template contains a check chunk that runs `ottr::check()` on that question.
    Run it to see the results of the **public checks**: quick tests that confirm your answer has the right structure (a fitted model, a data frame with the right columns, and so on).
    These checks are designed to tell you whether you're on the right track *without* revealing the answer.

3.  **The last check chunk checks your code style.**
    It reports any lines that do not follow the course style guidelines (see below), with line numbers, so you can fix them before submitting.

::: callout-note
## Multiple choice and short answers

Some questions ask you to record an answer by assigning a value to a variable.
Letters and names must be typed as strings (in quotes), for example `q2_why_not_linear <- "B"` or `q4_class <- "canceled"`.
Numeric answers are typed as numbers without quotes, for example `q5_TPR <- 0.5`.
:::

::: callout-warning
Passing all public checks does **not** guarantee full credit.
When your submission is graded, additional **hidden tests** check your answers for full correctness.
An answer with the right shape but wrong values can pass every public check and still lose points, so always sanity-check your results yourself.
A check chunk that errors with something like "object not found" usually means you haven't run the cells above it -- run all chunks in order (or render the document) and try again.
If your checks start failing after you re-run a chunk, restart R (**Session ➛ Restart R**) and run the chunks in order from the top.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Never put these in your document

`install.packages()`, `View()`, and `?` help requests belong in the Console, never in a code chunk.
A document containing them will fail the autograder.
:::

## Guidelines

Code should follow the [tidyverse style](https://style.tidyverse.org/).
Particularly,

-   there should be spaces before and line breaks after each `+` when building a `ggplot`,

-   there should also be spaces before and line breaks after each `|>` in a data transformation pipeline,

-   there should be spaces around `=` signs and spaces after commas.

Furthermore, all code should be visible in the PDF output, i.e., should not run off the page on the PDF.
Lines should not span more than 80 characters; long lines should be split across multiple lines with line breaks.[^1]

## Data

The dataset, called `hotels.csv`, can be found in the `data` folder.
The template reads it in with:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| message: false
hotels <- read_csv("data/hotels.csv")
```

The variables used in this lab are:

| Variable      | Description                                                                                         |
|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `hotel`       | Type of hotel: `City Hotel` or `Resort Hotel`                                                       |
| `is_canceled` | Whether the booking was canceled: `1` if canceled, `0` if not (the guests checked in)               |
| `lead_time`   | Number of days between the date the booking was made and the arrival date                           |
| `adults`      | Number of adults in the booking                                                                     |
| `adr`         | Average daily rate: the sum of all lodging transactions for the booking divided by the number of nights stayed, in dollars |


Below is an exploratory summary of some of the variables we will use in our analysis.

::: {layout="[0.55, -0.05, 0.4]"}

:::{#firstcol}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
hotels |>
  count(is_canceled) |>
  mutate(
    is_canceled = if_else(is_canceled == 1, "1 - Canceled", "0 - Not canceled")
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Cancellation status", "Number of bookings"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-asp: 0.55
ggplot(hotels, aes(x = lead_time)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  labs(
    x = "Days between booking and arrival",
    y = "Count",
    title = "lead_time: Days between booking and arrival"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-asp: 0.55
ggplot(hotels, aes(x = adr)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    x = "Average daily rate",
    title = "adr: Average daily rate",
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

:::


:::{#secondcol}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
hotels |>
  count(adults) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Number of adults", "Number of bookings"))
```

:::

# Questions

## Part 1 - Data prep

### Question 1

**1a.**
In a single pipeline starting from `hotels`, prepare the data for modeling and save the result as a new data frame named `hotels_clean`.
The pipeline should:

-   transform `is_canceled` to the appropriate data class so that it uses informative labels (`"not canceled"` and `"canceled"` instead of 0 and 1, respectively), with the levels ordered such that when we fit a logistic regression model to predict this outcome, success is defined as `"canceled"` (what we're predicting); and
-   based on the exploratory summaries above, address a few data quality issues by removing any bookings with average daily rate greater than \$1,000 and any bookings with number of adults greater than or equal to 5.

**1b.**
Split `hotels_clean` into a training set (75%) and a testing set (25%), setting the random seed to `1117` for reproducibility (the `set.seed(1117)` line is already in the template, immediately before the split).
Save the split as `hotels_split`, the training set as `hotels_train`, and the testing set as `hotels_test`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Render, commit, and push"}
Render, commit, and push your changes to GitHub with the commit message "Added answer for Question 1".

Make sure to commit and push all changed files so that your Git pane is empty afterward.
:::

## Part 2 - Predicting cancellations

Using these data, one of our goals is to explore the following question:

> *Are bookings made further in advance more likely to be canceled?*

The variable `lead_time` is the number of days between the date the booking was made and the arrival date.

### Question 2

**2a.**
In a single pipeline, calculate the number of bookings and the mean lead time for reservations that were canceled and reservations that were not canceled.
The result should have the columns `is_canceled`, `n`, and `mean_lead_time`.
Save it as `lead_by_cancel`.

::: callout-tip
Think carefully about which dataset you should use: `hotels_clean`, the training subset, or the testing subset?
:::

**2b.**
Record in `q2_why_not_linear` the option that best explains why we cannot use a linear model to model the relationship between whether a booking was canceled and its lead time:

   A. A linear model requires the outcome to be normally distributed, which a yes/no outcome is not.

   B. A linear model can only be fit when the predictor is categorical, and lead time is numeric.

   C. A linear model would produce predicted values outside 0 to 1, which cannot be probabilities.

   D. A linear model cannot be fit to a dataset with as many observations as this one has.

### Question 3

**3a.**
Fit a logistic regression model to predict whether a booking was canceled from `lead_time`, using the **training set**, and save it as `cancel_fit`.
Display a tidy summary of the model output (`tidy(cancel_fit)` is already in the template).

**3b.**
Record in `q3_slope_interp` the option that correctly interprets the slope coefficient.
The model predicts that, for each additional day of lead time, ...

   A. the probability of cancellation is higher by a factor of about 1.006, on average.

   B. the odds of cancellation are higher by a factor of about 1.006, on average.

   C. the odds of cancellation are higher by a factor of about 0.006, on average.

   D. the odds of cancellation are lower by a factor of about 1.006, on average.

::: {.callout-tip title="Render, commit, and push"}
Render, commit, and push your changes to GitHub with the commit message "Added answers for Questions 2 and 3".

Make sure to commit and push all changed files so that your Git pane is empty afterward.
:::

### Question 4

Consider a booking made **300 days** in advance.

Let $b_0$ be the estimated intercept and $b_1$ the estimated slope from `cancel_fit`.

**4a.**
Record in `q4_formula` which of the following expressions gives the predicted probability that this booking is canceled:

   A. $b_0 + b_1 \times 300$

   B. $e^{\,b_0 + b_1 \times 300}$

   C. $\dfrac{1 + e^{\,b_0 + b_1 \times 300}}{e^{\,b_0 + b_1 \times 300}}$

   D. $\dfrac{e^{\,b_0 + b_1 \times 300}}{1 + e^{\,b_0 + b_1 \times 300}}$

**4b.**
Compute this probability *by hand* using the coefficients from your tidy output, and record it in `q4_prob_hand` as a number.
(You may do the arithmetic in R, but write out the formula yourself rather than calling `predict()`.)

**4c.**
Now compute the same probability with R, using `predict()` and `type = "prob"` with a new data frame containing `lead_time = 300`.
Save the result as `q4_prob_r`; the probability of cancellation is in its `.pred_canceled` column.
It should agree with your by-hand value up to rounding.

**4d.**
Using a probability threshold of 0.5, record the model's classification of this booking in `q4_class`, as the string `"canceled"` or `"not canceled"`.

**4e.**
It turns out that this booking was actually canceled. Given that fact and the model's classification, record in `q4_outcome_type` which of the following this booking is:

   A. a true positive

   B. a false positive

   C. a true negative

   D. a false negative

### Question 5

**5a.**
Use `augment()` to add predicted classes and probabilities to the **testing** set, and save the result as `cancel_pred`.
The predicted class is in the `.pred_class` column.

**5b.**
From `cancel_pred`, compute the following rates as proportions between 0 and 1, and record them in `q5_TPR`, `q5_FPR`, `q5_TNR`, and `q5_FNR`:

-   **True positive rate (TPR):** of the bookings that were actually canceled, the proportion the model predicted to be canceled.
-   **False positive rate (FPR):** of the bookings that were actually not canceled, the proportion the model predicted to be canceled.
-   **True negative rate (TNR):** of the bookings that were actually not canceled, the proportion the model predicted to be not canceled.
-   **False negative rate (FNR):** of the bookings that were actually canceled, the proportion the model predicted to be not canceled.

**5c.**
Record in `q5_interp` the option that best describes what these rates say about the model:

   A. The model correctly identifies most of the bookings that were actually canceled.

   B. The model correctly identifies only a minority of the bookings that were actually canceled.

   C. The model predicts cancellation for most of the bookings that were not actually canceled.

   D. The model never predicts cancellation, so it misses every booking that was actually canceled.

Render, commit, and push your changes to GitHub with the commit message "Added answers for Questions 4 and 5".

Make sure to commit and push all changed files so that your Git pane is empty afterward.
:::

### Question 6

**6a.**
Fit another model to predict whether a booking was canceled from `lead_time` and `hotel` type (Resort Hotel or City Hotel), with main effects only (no interaction), using the training set.
Save it as `cancel_hotel_fit` and display a tidy output of the model.

**6b.**
Record in `q6_intercept_interp` the option that correctly interprets the intercept:

   A. For a City Hotel booking made 0 days in advance, the predicted probability of cancellation is about $\dfrac{e^{-0.99}}{1+e^{-0.99}}\approx 0.27$.

   B. For a Resort Hotel booking made 0 days in advance, the predicted probability of cancellation is about $\dfrac{e^{-0.99}}{1+e^{-0.99}}\approx 0.27$.

   C. For a City Hotel booking made 0 days in advance, the predicted probability of cancellation is about $-0.99$.

   D. For each additional day of lead time at a Resort Hotel, the predicted odds of cancellation change by a factor of about $e^{-0.99} \approx 0.37$.

## Part 3 - Predicting daily rates

### Question 7

The dataset also contains information about the average daily rate (`adr`) for each booking.
The following multiple linear regression model, fit on the training set, predicts `adr` from `adults` and `hotel` type.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| message: false
hotels_clean <- hotels |>
  filter(adr <= 1000, adults < 5)
set.seed(1117)
hotels_split <- initial_split(hotels_clean)
hotels_train <- training(hotels_split)
```


```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
adr_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(adr ~ adults + hotel, data = hotels_train)

tidy(adr_fit)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
adr_coefs <- tidy(adr_fit)
b_int <- sprintf("%.2f", adr_coefs$estimate[adr_coefs$term == "(Intercept)"])
b_adults <- sprintf("%.2f", adr_coefs$estimate[adr_coefs$term == "adults"])
b_hotel <- sprintf("%.2f", abs(adr_coefs$estimate[adr_coefs$term == "hotelResort Hotel"]))
```

**7a.**
Record in `q7_adults` the best interpretation of the slope coefficient for `adults`.
For each additional adult in the booking, the average daily rate is predicted to be higher by \$29.70

   A. for Resort Hotels compared to City Hotels, on average.

   B. for City Hotels compared to Resort Hotels, on average.

   C. on average, without holding hotel type constant.

   D. on average, holding hotel type constant.

**7b.**
Record in `q7_hotel` the correct interpretation of the slope coefficient for `hotel`:

   A. For each additional Resort Hotel booking, the predicted average daily rate is \$10.90 lower, holding number of adults constant.

   B. For each additional adult in the booking, the predicted average daily rate is \$10.90 lower at Resort Hotels than at City Hotels, on average.

   C. Resort Hotel bookings are predicted to have an average daily rate \$10.90 lower than City Hotel bookings, on average, holding number of adults constant.

   D. Resort Hotel bookings are predicted to have an average daily rate \$10.90 higher than City Hotel bookings, on average, holding number of adults constant.

**7c.**
Record in `q7_intercept` the correct interpretation of the intercept:

   A. The predicted average daily rate for a booking with 0 adults at a Resort Hotel is \$50.30.

   B. The predicted average daily rate for a booking with 0 adults at a City Hotel is \$50.30.

   C. For each additional adult at a City Hotel, the average daily rate is predicted to be \$50.30 higher.

   D. The predicted average daily rate for a booking with 1 adult at a City Hotel is \$50.30.

**7d.**
Which of the following (Plot A or Plot B) is the correct visual representation of this model?
Record your answer in `q7_plot` as `"A"` or `"B"`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| message: false
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-asp: 0.618
adr_aug <- augment(adr_fit, new_data = hotels_train)

ggplot(hotels_train, aes(x = adults, y = adr, color = hotel)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 1, se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Plot A",
    x = "Number of adults",
    y = "Average daily rate",
    color = "Hotel"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.15, 0.80))

ggplot(adr_aug, aes(x = adults, color = hotel)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = adr)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .pred), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Plot B",
    x = "Number of adults",
    y = "Average daily rate",
    color = "Hotel"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.15, 0.80))
```

::: callout-tip
Think about whether a model with only the main effects of `adults` and `hotel`, or one that also includes their interaction, produces lines with the same slope for both hotel types.
:::
